lines.t: Hoo! Welcome to the night market, {name}. The clock chimed this morning: the Golem comes in 30 hours.
Tonight the market hangs its lanterns. Every lantern needs a ribbon, and the ribbons are measured in parts of a foot.
That's Ivy, the lantern-keeper, at the ribbon stall. She looks worried. Go say hello.
Hoo! The Math Crew worked out Ivy's ribbon puzzle. They each found the answer their own way.
Walk up to each of them and listen. Then come back and tell me.
Hoo! Two ways, and one answer: five sixths of a foot is 10 inches.
Which way is most like yours? Write about it on your page, right under the Crew's card.
Walk up to each Crew member and listen to their way first.
The factory is found. Tomorrow the farmers' market, {name}, and the Golem.
Hoo! Every lantern job on the page helps Ivy light the night market.
Hoo! Part 1 at the dairy, part 2 here. The Golem is being built, {name}.
Tomorrow, the farmers' market. We'll be ready for it.

lines.t: Seven times 1,000 is 7,000. But a tenth means the liter is cut into 10 equal parts. One part is 100 milliliters.
Four times 1,000 is 4,000. A fourth is one of 4 equal parts of the liter, so it is smaller than 1,000.
Here is my rule for going backward, from inches to a fraction of a foot.
The part and the whole must be in the same unit. 10 inches out of a foot is 10 inches out of 12 inches, never 10 out of 1.
That's what the Smudge wrote! A third of an hour isn't 3 minutes. An hour is 60 minutes. Cut 60 into 3 equal parts.
This tag is about a pound of tea, not a foot. A pound is 16 ounces. One fourth of 16 ounces is how many ounces?
Hello, I'm Cora. Every ribbon here has a tag, and some of the tags look smudged. I don't trust them.
Going backward, write the part over the whole in the same unit. Then make bigger equal parts to simplify.

lines.t: That is one tenth. Ivy wants 7 of them.
Cut 1,000 milliliters into 10 equal parts. One part is 100. Take 7 parts.
Close! A liter is 1,000 milliliters, not 100. Cut 1,000 into 4 equal parts.
Cut 1,000 milliliters into 4 equal parts. How big is one part?
My way is to cut the foot into equal parts first.
Sixths means 6 equal parts. 12 inches cut into 6 equal parts is 2 inches each.
Then I take 5 of the parts. 5 times 2 inches is 10 inches. Same answer as Atlas!
A fraction of a unit is a fraction of its small units. One third of a foot is one third of 12 inches.
3 times 60 is 180. But a third is one of 3 equal parts of the hour, so it is less than 60 minutes.
An hour is 60 minutes. A third means 3 equal parts. How many minutes in one part?
Hey, I'm Felix! I counted the hooks on the lantern string. Every one of them is empty.
I cut the whole into equal parts first. Twelfths means 12 parts of 1 inch each. Seven parts is 7 inches.

lines.t: Picture the meter cut in half. Half of 100 centimeters is less than 100, not more.
I picture a foot ruler with its 12 inch marks.
If I cut it into 6 equal pieces, every piece is 2 inches long. Five of those pieces reach 10 inches, just 2 inches short of the end.
Hi! I'm Hazel. I'm drawing Ivy's ribbon stall. Look at all the colors!
I picture the ruler cut into equal pieces. Then I count the pieces I need.

lines.t: A meter is 100 centimeters. Half means 2 equal parts.
My way is to multiply the fraction by 12, because a foot is 12 inches.
Five sixths times 12. First 5 times 12, that's 60. Then 60 divided by 6, that's 10.
So five sixths of a foot is 10 inches!
Hi, I'm Atlas! A night market! I've never seen so many lanterns in one place. Well, I will, once they're hung.
To find a fraction of a unit, I multiply the fraction by the number of small units. Five sixths of a foot is 5 times 12, that's 60, divided by 6: 10 inches.

lines.t: Oh, hello! I'm Ivy. I keep the lanterns for the night market.
The Smudge tipped over my tag box, and the tags blew all over the square. Each tag names a fraction of a unit.
Please sort them into my bins. Each bin is an amount: 4 inches, 5 inches, 6 inches or 4 ounces. Walk onto a sparkle to pick up a tag.
Every tag is in its bin. Thank you, {name}!
The lantern string is still empty, and it's getting dark!
Here are three ribbons. Each tag is a fraction of a foot, but my ruler only shows inches.
Walk to the lantern string and cut each ribbon to the right number of inches.
The lanterns light up the whole square now. And look, behind the market!
There is gray dust on the ground in the alley. Brick dust. Follow it, {name}!
Welcome to the night market! Ribbons, lanterns and tea. Everything here comes in parts of a unit.
They're beautiful! Thank you, {name}.
